Toxicokinetics
Absorption of lead from the digestive tract is highly variable and relatively low (10–20%). Pregnant women and children (who are
more susceptible to the toxic effects of lead) may absorb a higher amount and this depends on the nutritional status (levels of
calcium, phosphate or iron can inﬂuence their uptake). Once absorbed, it is distributed in blood bound to erythrocytes
(>95%), most likely due to its high afﬁnity for delta-amino levulinic acid dehydratase, leaving a small fraction in plasma. It accu-
mulates in the epiphysis of long bones (e.g., femur, tibia and humerus), being eliminated mainly through urine (75%), to a lesser
extent through feces and also through nails and hair.
